source: multi-agent audit 2026-07-16 (workflow stopped early; verification phase incomplete)
status: UNVERIFIED CANDIDATES — each needs adversarial verification before fixing; finder claims may be wrong or already handled elsewhere

candidates.title: enforce_token_limit's 1.5-chars/token estimate silently truncates chunks the exact BERT tokenizer already verified as in-budget (recommended Ollama path)
candidates.failure_scenario: With the `tokenizers` gem installed (which TokenCounter's warning explicitly tells users to do), SemanticChunker#oversize? uses ONLY the exact token check (`return @token_counter.count(content) > @max_tokens if tokenizer_active?`, semantic_chunker.rb:144) and bypasses max_chars — so chunks legitimately grow to 1792 real BERT tokens ≈ 4500-5400 chars of normal Ruby (~2.5-3 chars/BERT-token). TextPreparer (built with max_tokens=2048, chars_per_token=1.5 via Builder#build_text_preparer) then estimates `len/1.5` tokens and truncates any prepared text over 3072 chars. Every tokenizer-approved chunk between ~3072 and ~5400 chars silently loses its tail from the embedding — the exact-sizing feature is defeated by the crude estimate downstream, degrading retrieval with no warning. Verified empirically: a 3800-char chunk (well under 1792 BERT tokens) came back from prepare_chunks at exactly 3072 chars, truncated=true. Without the tokenizers gem the numbers coincidentally line up (2560-char chunks + 512 prefix = 3072, no truncation), so only the documented best-practice config is harmed.
candidates.evidence: text_preparer.rb:129-133 `estimated = (text.length / @chars_per_token).ceil; return text if estimated <= @max_tokens; max_chars = (@max_tokens * @chars_per_token).floor; text[0...max_chars]`; semantic_chunker.rb:144 token check bypasses char limit; scratchpad run: `{:chunk_chars=>3800, :prepared_chars=>3072, :truncated=>true}`.
candidates.suggested_fix: When the pipeline has an exact TokenCounter, give TextPreparer the same counter (or skip char-estimate truncation for pre-verified chunk texts) and only truncate on a real over-budget count; at minimum warn when truncating so the loss isn't silent.

candidates.title: Chunker depth tracking only counts `do`/`def` openers but decrements on every bare `end` — actions/methods containing if/unless/case/while blocks are closed early and mis-chunked
candidates.failure_scenario: ControllerChunker#track_action_line increments depth only for `\bdo\b` lines, yet decrements on any line matching `/^end\s*$/`. A bog-standard action `def show; @post = ...; if @post.archived?; redirect_to root_path; end; render :show; end` hits the inner `if`'s `end` at depth 1, decrements to 0, and closes the action. Verified empirically: the `action_show` chunk ends at the inner `end`, while `render :show` and the method's real `end` leak into the `:summary` chunk (output: summary contains 'render :show / end / end'). Any controller action or MethodChunker/ModelChunker method containing a multi-line if/unless/case/while/begin — i.e. most real Rails code — produces truncated per-action/per-method embeddings and a summary chunk polluted with dangling body fragments, degrading chunk-level retrieval precision for exactly the units the semantic chunker exists to improve.
candidates.evidence: semantic_chunker.rb:463-467 `state[:depth] += 1 if line.match?(/\bdo\b/) && !line.match?(/\bend\b/) ... return unless line.strip.match?(/^end\s*$/); state[:depth] -= 1`; same pattern at 565-569 (MethodChunker) and 377-378 (ModelChunker, which adds only `def`). Scratchpad run shows `action_show` chunk cut mid-method.
candidates.suggested_fix: Count all block openers (if/unless/case/while/until/begin/class/module at expression position, excluding trailing modifiers — reuse RakeTaskExtractor's `block_opener?` line-start heuristic) when incrementing depth, or switch these chunkers to the existing Prism AST layer for boundary detection.

candidates.title: Re-embedding a changed unit never deletes stale chunk vectors — shrinking chunk counts leave orphaned `#chunk_N` embeddings in persistent stores
candidates.failure_scenario: Chunk vector ids are positional: `embed_id = texts.length > 1 ? "#{identifier}#chunk_#{idx}" : identifier`. store_vectors only calls `@vector_store.store_batch` (upsert by id); nothing in indexer.rb ever calls the stores' `delete`/`delete_by_filter`. Run 1: `User` embeds as 5 chunks (`User#chunk_0..4`). The model shrinks; incremental run 2 embeds 2 chunks, upserting `#chunk_0/#chunk_1` — but `User#chunk_2..4`, embedding source code that no longer exists, remain in pgvector/Qdrant forever and keep matching semantic queries (their metadata identifier resolves to the current unit, so retrieval serves the fresh metadata for a hit earned by deleted code — silent ranking corruption). A unit dropping to a single prepared text is worse: it's stored under the bare `identifier` while ALL old `#chunk_*` rows linger. The checkpoint marks the unit done (`checkpoint[item[:identifier]] = item[:source_hash]`), so no later run cleans up; the vector index grows and drifts stale across every incremental cycle. In-memory-store specs never notice because the snapshot path rewrites the whole dump.
candidates.evidence: indexer.rb:142 `embed_id = texts.length > 1 ? "#{identifier}#chunk_#{idx}" : identifier`; indexer.rb:241-253 store_vectors calls only `@vector_store.store_batch(entries)` then advances the checkpoint; `grep delete lib/woods/embedding/indexer.rb` → no matches, while pgvector.rb:125/131 expose unused `delete`/`delete_by_filter`.
candidates.suggested_fix: Before storing a re-embedded unit's entries, delete its prior vectors (e.g. `delete_by_filter(identifier: ...)` or track last chunk count in the checkpoint and delete `#chunk_{new_n..old_n-1}` plus the bare id / chunked ids on shape changes).

candidates.title: embed_and_store sends all chunk texts of a 32-unit batch in one HTTP request — no cap, violating OpenAI's 2048-input / 300k-total-token per-request limits
candidates.failure_scenario: `@batch_size` slices UNITS, but collect_embed_items fans each unit out into one item per chunk, and embed_and_store passes the entire accumulated list to a single `provider.embed_batch` → one POST to /v1/embeddings. The real OpenAI API caps an embeddings request at 2048 input items and ~300k total tokens (400: 'max 300000 tokens per request'). Pre-chunked framework units (`woods:extract_framework` rails_source, which the Indexer comment at line 151-153 explicitly anticipates as oversized) carry many ~8k-token chunks each; 32 such units in one slice easily exceeds 300k total tokens (e.g. 32 units × 5 chunks × 8k tokens ≈ 1.3M), so the request 400s and `rescue StandardError` re-raises `Woods::Error, "Embedding failed: ..."` — aborting the entire woods:embed run partway with up to 10 batches of un-checkpointed progress lost. The spec fake is unfaithful to this contract: indexer_spec.rb:28-31's `embed_batch(texts)` returns `Array.new(texts.length) { @vector }` for any size, so no spec can catch it — the same fake-vs-real gap class as the run_git newline bug.
candidates.evidence: indexer.rb:234 `vectors = @provider.embed_batch(items.map { |i| i[:text] })` fed by process_batch (lines 105-120) which accumulates every chunk of up to 32 units; openai.rb:68 `post_request({ model: @model, input: texts })` sends them as one request with no size guard; spec/embedding/indexer_spec.rb:28-31 fake accepts unbounded arrays.
candidates.suggested_fix: In embed_and_store (or the providers), split items into sub-requests bounded by the provider's real per-request limits (OpenAI: ≤2048 inputs and ≤~300k estimated total tokens; expose as `max_batch_inputs`/`max_batch_tokens` on the Interface) and concatenate the vectors in order.

candidates.title: parse_idx returns vector ids as ASCII-8BIT strings — non-ASCII identifiers fail every hash/equality lookup after snapshot reload
candidates.failure_scenario: The idx format documents ids as UTF-8, but load goes File.binread → byteslice, which yields ASCII-8BIT strings without re-tagging. For ASCII-only ids this is invisible (compatible encodings hash equal), but any identifier containing non-ASCII bytes (e.g. class Café, an i18n view/template path baked into a unit id) round-trips as a binary string that is neither == nor eql? to its UTF-8 original. Verified empirically: after dump+load, id encoding is ASCII-8BIT and a metadata hash keyed 'Café::Menü' returns nil for the loaded id while 'User' resolves. Consequence: populate_vector_metadata's metadata_store.find misses (unit keeps empty metadata), and ContextAssembler#find_batch on the returned SearchResult#id misses too, so the unit silently vanishes from retrieval results after any server restart — same code works in the fresh embed process.
candidates.evidence: vector.rb:122-131: `idx_data = File.binread(idx_path.to_s)` ... `id = idx_data.byteslice(pos, id_len)` — no force_encoding, while the writer explicitly encodes UTF-8 (`id_bytes = id.encode('UTF-8').b`, line 196). Repro output: `id="Caf\xC3\xA9::Men\xC3\xBC" enc=ASCII-8BIT` and `find(...) -> nil` vs `find("User") -> {...}`.
candidates.suggested_fix: In parse_idx, tag the sliced bytes back to the declared format encoding: `id = idx_data.byteslice(pos, id_len).force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8)` (and consider `.freeze`); add a round-trip spec with a non-ASCII identifier.

candidates.title: Snapshot dumps are written with Tempfile's 0600 mode (and downgrade existing 0644 files), making them unreadable across the documented container-writes/host-reads deployment
candidates.failure_scenario: atomic_write creates the payload via Tempfile (always mode 0600 regardless of umask) and File.rename preserves that mode — verified empirically: overwriting a pre-existing 0644 vectors.bin leaves it 0600 even with umask 022. In the documented Docker workflow (CLAUDE.md/docs: extraction+embed run inside the container, typically as root; the Index Server runs on the host as a different UID reading the volume-mounted output), vectors.bin/vectors.idx/metadata.msgpack become root-owned 0600, so the host woods-mcp process gets EACCES on File.binread. Bootstrapper rescues StandardError and merely warns 'vector hydration failed ... starting with empty store' (bootstrapper.rb:423), so the server silently serves zero vectors/metadata instead of failing loudly. Snapshotter::Metadata.write_atomic (metadata.rb:132) and the shared Woods::AtomicFile (atomic_file.rb:29, used for all index JSON) have the identical flaw, so the whole artifact tree flips to 0600.
candidates.evidence: vector.rb:204-212 `tmp = Tempfile.new('.woods-vec-', path.dirname.to_s) ... File.rename(tmp.path, path.to_s)` — no chmod between create and rename. Repro: `mode after snapshotter atomic_write: 600` with `umask: 0022`, starting from a 0644 destination file.
candidates.suggested_fix: Before rename, restore conventional permissions: `File.chmod(File.stat(path).mode & 0o777, tmp.path) rescue File.chmod(0o666 & ~File.umask, tmp.path)` (mirroring ActiveSupport's File.atomic_write), applied in both Snapshotter writers and Woods::AtomicFile.

candidates.title: SchemaVersion/Migrator claim pg and mysql2 compatibility but emit SQLite-only SQL — ensure_table! and record_version fail immediately on PostgreSQL or MySQL
candidates.failure_scenario: The class doc says 'Works with any database connection that supports execute and returns arrays (SQLite3, pg, mysql2)' and the Migrator example encourages passing an arbitrary connection. A user wiring their PG/MySQL connection (as the storage rules require: 'MySQL and PostgreSQL adapters are first-class citizens', 'Never write PostgreSQL-only SQL' — here it is SQLite-only): ensure_table! executes DEFAULT (datetime('now')) — PG raises 'function datetime(unknown) does not exist' at CREATE TABLE, MySQL rejects the expression; record_version uses 'INSERT OR IGNORE' (SQLite dialect; MySQL needs INSERT IGNORE, PG needs ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) and passes bind params as execute's second positional arg, which PG#execute/Mysql2::Client#query do not accept. Migrations compound it: AUTOINCREMENT (001-005) and sqlite_master (006_rename_tables.rb:24) are SQLite-only. In-gem callers currently always pass SQLite3::Database, so this only fires for doc-following external use — but every temporal-snapshot code path is dialect-locked despite the backend-agnostic contract.
candidates.evidence: schema_version.rb:8-9 doc: 'Works with any database connection ... (SQLite3, pg, mysql2)'; :34 `applied_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))`; :53 `"INSERT OR IGNORE INTO #{TABLE_NAME} (version) VALUES (?)", [version]`; migrations/006_rename_tables.rb:24 `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='#{old_name}'`.
candidates.suggested_fix: Either correct the docs/YARD to state SQLite-only and guard Migrator with an adapter check, or implement per-dialect SQL (portable DEFAULT via application-supplied timestamps, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT/IGNORE per adapter, information_schema instead of sqlite_master) as the backend matrix requires.

candidates.title: PageRank importance map memoized forever on the Ranker instance — MCP `reload` tool leaves importance scoring stale or permanently empty
candidates.failure_scenario: Retriever creates one Ranker at initialize and retriever.rb:92-98 documents that in-place `clear!` + `bulk_load` (Bootstrapper.reload_stores!, used by the MCP `reload` tool) 'propagates through the entire pipeline without re-instantiating sub-components'. But the first rank() call memoizes `@pagerank_importance_map` from the graph store's then-current contents. Sequence: woods-mcp boots before/with an old embed → agent runs any retrieve (memoizes {} or stale percentiles) → operator runs woods:embed → agent calls `reload` → graph store now holds fresh pagerank, yet every subsequent query keeps scoring importance from the pre-reload snapshot: new units silently fall back to bucketed metadata, deleted units keep ghost percentiles. Also `compute_pagerank_importance_map` rescues StandardError to {} — a single transient graph-store error on the first query permanently disables the PageRank signal for the process lifetime because `||=` memoizes the truthy empty hash. Empirically verified: after simulating reload (graph store gains 2 pagerank entries), `ranker.pagerank_importance_map` still returns {}.
candidates.evidence: ranker.rb:229: `@pagerank_importance_map ||= compute_pagerank_importance_map`; ranker.rb:246-247: `rescue StandardError` / `{}`; retriever.rb:96-98: "in-place +#clear!+ + +#bulk_load+ propagates through the entire pipeline without re-instantiating sub-components". Scratchpad run: "after reload, ranker pagerank map: {} (graph store now has 2 entries)".
candidates.suggested_fix: Don't memoize across store mutations: recompute per rank() call (it's a sort of an in-memory hash), key the memo on a store version/fingerprint, or expose Ranker#reset_cache! and invoke it from Bootstrapper.reload_stores!. Also stop memoizing the rescue-path {} so a transient error doesn't disable the signal permanently.

candidates.title: Framework candidates assembled twice — full unit source duplicated in both :primary and :framework sections, hidden by sources.uniq
candidates.failure_scenario: On any framework-context query (framework_query? matches bare 'rails', 'activerecord', 'middleware', etc.), a rails_source/gem_source candidate from vector or keyword search passes the :primary filter (it is not :graph_expansion) AND the :framework filter (framework_candidate?), so format_unit emits its complete source text twice in one assembled context. Framework units are the largest in the index (chunked Rails internals), so up to primary(55%) + framework(20%) of the post-structural budget is spent on identical content, crowding out app code — and `sources.uniq` (context_assembler.rb:359) collapses the two identical attribution hashes so the duplication is invisible to callers auditing sources. Empirically verified: one rails_source candidate with framework_context=true produces sections [:primary, :framework], the '## ActiveRecord::Persistence' header appears 2 times in the context, sources reports 1.
candidates.evidence: context_assembler.rb:112-118: `add_candidate_section(sections, sources, :primary, candidates.reject { |c| c.source == :graph_expansion }, budgets[:primary])` ... `add_candidate_section(sections, sources, :framework, candidates.select { |c| framework_candidate?(c) }, budgets[:framework])`. Scratchpad run: "sections: [:primary, :framework] / occurrences of unit header in context: 2 / sources: 1".
candidates.suggested_fix: Exclude framework candidates from the primary pool when the framework section will be assembled: `candidates.reject { |c| c.source == :graph_expansion || (budgets[:framework].positive? && framework_candidate?(c)) }`.

candidates.title: Ranker looks up metadata with raw chunked identifiers (Foo#chunk_N) — chunked candidates score neutral on every metadata signal
candidates.failure_scenario: Chunked vector hits arrive as `User#chunk_0` but the metadata store is keyed by base identifier only — Retriever#candidate_type (retriever.rb:264) and ContextAssembler#base_identifier (context_assembler.rb:136) both strip CHUNK_SUFFIX_PATTERN for exactly this reason, with comments stating the store 'is keyed by the base identifier'. Ranker#score_candidates passes raw identifiers to find_batch, so `unit` is nil for every chunked candidate: recency/importance/type_match all pin at the 0.5 fallback and diversity_penalty_for returns nil (chunked units never accumulate namespace/type counts). Concrete effect: query 'how does the payment model work' with target_type :model — an unchunked wrong-type unit gets type_match 0.3 while a chunked candidate of the CORRECT type gets 0.5 instead of 1.0, losing its rightful 0.05 weighted bonus; hot/high chunked units similarly lose up to 0.125 weighted score vs their true metadata, systematically mis-ranking large units (rails_source, big models) relative to small ones.
candidates.evidence: ranker.rb:135: `unit_map = @metadata_store.find_batch(candidates.map(&:identifier))` (no suffix strip), vs retriever.rb:263-265: "a missed lookup would let the candidate past the default-exclude" / `lookup_id = candidate.identifier.to_s.sub(CHUNK_SUFFIX_PATTERN, '')` and context_assembler.rb:130: `CHUNK_SUFFIX_PATTERN = /#chunk_\d+\z/` with the collapse rationale at lines 95-99.
candidates.suggested_fix: In score_candidates, resolve metadata through the base identifier: `unit_map = @metadata_store.find_batch(candidates.map { |c| c.identifier.to_s.sub(CHUNK_SUFFIX_PATTERN, '') })` and index lookups the same way (mirroring Retriever's private CHUNK_SUFFIX_PATTERN copy), so chunked candidates inherit their unit's recency/importance/type/namespace signals.

candidates.title: Columns sync upserts by bare column name — every model's shared-name columns (created_at, updated_at, id, ...) collapse into one Notion page that flip-flops between models each run
candidates.failure_scenario: Host app has Post and Comment, both with created_at (true of every Rails model). sync_columns pushes Post.created_at (page created, Table relation -> posts, Nullable=false). For Comment.created_at, upsert_page -> find_page_by_title(title: 'created_at') matches Post's page against the REAL Notion API, and update_page overwrites it: Table relation now -> comments, Nullable flipped. Verified empirically with a faithful fake (scratchpad/notion_collision_test.rb): stats report columns: 3 synced, but only 2 pages exist and Post's created_at data is gone. In a real app the Columns DB degenerates to one page per distinct column name org-wide, contents owned by whichever model synced last, rewritten every run — silent cross-model data corruption while counts look healthy. Same mechanism corrupts sync_data_models for STI models (title = shared table_name). Invisible to specs because spec/notion/exporter_spec.rb:91 stubs find_page_by_title to always return nil (fake diverges from real find-by-title contract), so tests only ever exercise the create path.
candidates.evidence: exporter.rb:152 `upsert_page(database_id: database_id, title_value: column['name'], properties: properties)`; upsert_page (lines 186-196) does `existing = @client.find_page_by_title(database_id:, title: title_value); if existing @client.update_page(page_id: existing['id'], ...)`; mappers/column_mapper.rb:29 `'Column Name' => { title: [{ text: { content: column['name'] } }] }` (title is the bare column name; docs/NOTION_INTEGRATION.md line 61 confirms 'Column Name | Title'); spec/notion/exporter_spec.rb:91 `allow(client).to receive(:find_page_by_title).and_return(nil)`
candidates.suggested_fix: Make the column page identity model-scoped: set the title to "#{model_identifier}.#{column['name']}" in ColumnMapper (and pass the same value as title_value at exporter.rb:152), or keep the bare title but find existing pages by (title AND Table relation == parent_page_id). Add a spec whose fake find_page_by_title actually matches previously created titles.

candidates.title: 'Last Schema Change' uses the unit's extraction wall-clock timestamp instead of the migration's version date — every table shows the date of the last woods:extract run
candidates.failure_scenario: users table last migrated in 2021, posts migrated yesterday. Run `woods:extract` then `woods:notion_sync`: every migration ExtractedUnit gets extracted_at = Time.now.iso8601 at extraction time (all within the same run, seconds apart), so latest_changes returns ~the extraction timestamp for every table, and both users and posts show 'Last Schema Change: today'. The property is permanently wrong for all tables and re-wrong after each extraction — the feature (docs/NOTION_INTEGRATION.md line 18: 'Last schema change (from migration history)') never reports migration history. The real schema-change date is extracted and available in metadata['migration_version'] (migration filename timestamp, migration_extractor.rb:167) but never read. Secondary defect: line 34 compares ISO8601 strings lexically, and Time.now.iso8601 carries the local UTC offset, so '2026-07-16T01:00:00+09:00' vs '2026-07-15T20:00:00Z' compares in the wrong chronological order across mixed-offset extractions.
candidates.evidence: migration_mapper.rb:22-26 `extracted_at = unit['extracted_at'] ... tables.each { |table| update_latest(changes, table, extracted_at) }` and :34 `changes[table] = extracted_at if changes[table].nil? || extracted_at > changes[table]`; extracted_unit.rb:59 `extracted_at: Time.now.iso8601,`; extractors/migration_extractor.rb:167 `migration_version: extract_migration_version(file_path),` (unused by the mapper)
candidates.suggested_fix: Read `unit.dig('metadata', 'migration_version')` (the 14-digit filename timestamp, e.g. '20240115093000'), parse it to a date for the Notion date property, and compare versions numerically/lexically on that fixed-width form; fall back to skipping units without a version rather than using extracted_at.

candidates.title: Unblocked sync deletes live remote documents for units whose per-unit JSON fails to load — skipped units are never tracked as current, so purge_stale treats them as orphans
candidates.failure_scenario: `woods:unblocked_sync` runs while a full extraction is rewriting the output dir (each _index.json and unit file is a separate atomic write, so there is a window where the index lists a unit whose JSON file is absent), or any single unit file is missing/corrupt-renamed. find_unit returns nil, the unit is counted 'skipped', and track_uri is never called — its URI is absent from @current_uris. purge_stale (line 274) then classifies the manifest entry as stale and DELETEs the still-valid remote document, reporting it under normal-looking 'skipped' and 'deleted' counts. Below the 30% guard threshold this proceeds silently; the document only reappears on the next run (costing budget). The same drop exists in sync_type_partial: line 151 `next unless data` filters unreadable units out BEFORE the line-160 loop whose whole comment says it exists so units are 'never mistaken for deletions'. The skill mandates serializing concurrent sync runs but says nothing about extract-vs-sync overlap, which is the realistic CI trigger.
candidates.evidence: exporter.rb:182-188 `unit_data = @reader.find_unit(entry['identifier']); unless unit_data; skipped += 1; next; end; track_uri(unit_data)` — no track on the nil path; exporter.rb:274 `stale = @manifest.stale_uris(@current_uris)` then :285 `@client.delete_document(document_id: document_id)`; sync_type_partial exporter.rb:151-153 `data = @reader.find_unit(entry['identifier']); next unless data` before the :160 track loop; mcp/index_reader.rb:534-535 `return nil unless path.file?` (listed-but-missing file yields nil)
candidates.suggested_fix: When an index entry has a file_path but its unit JSON cannot be loaded, still mark its URI current (entries carry file_path — call track_uri(entry), matching build_uri_index which already uses entry hashes), or set a @load_failures flag that skips purge_stale for the run, mirroring the @budget_exhausted purge skip.

candidates.title: Columns-only Notion configuration silently syncs nothing — sync_columns is gated on the data_models database ID too, contradicting the documented 'only one database ID' behavior
candidates.failure_scenario: User configures `notion_database_ids = { columns: 'db-uuid' }` (no data_models DB — CLAUDE.md promises 'If only one database ID is set, the other sync is skipped gracefully'). sync_all evaluates `@database_ids[:columns] && @database_ids[:data_models]` -> false, so the columns sync itself is skipped: the rake task reports success with `columns: 0, errors: []` and no message every run, and the user's Columns database stays empty with no indication why. The gate is not functionally required: ColumnMapper already handles a nil parent (`properties['Table'] = { relation: ... } if parent_page_id`), so column pages could sync without relations, and sync_columns is also a public method whose direct call works without data_models.
candidates.evidence: exporter.rb:48 `column_stats = @database_ids[:columns] && @database_ids[:data_models] ? sync_columns : empty_stats`; column_mapper.rb `properties['Table'] = { relation: [{ id: parent_page_id }] } if parent_page_id` (nil-safe); CLAUDE.md: 'If only one database ID is set, the other sync (columns or data_models) is skipped gracefully.'
candidates.suggested_fix: Gate sync_columns only on @database_ids[:columns] (relations degrade gracefully when the parent DB/page cache is absent), or if the double-gate is intentional, log an explicit warning ('columns database configured but data_models missing — columns sync skipped') instead of returning silent empty stats.

candidates.title: Foreign-vault export silently overwrites the user's own notes while claiming to write 'additively'
candidates.failure_scenario: A user points WOODS_OBSIDIAN_PATH at their existing personal vault (no .woods-vault sentinel — the exact case the ownership guard exists for). They have a handwritten note at models/User.md. export_all computes owned=false, correctly skips config and sweep, but write_notes runs unconditionally and AtomicFile.write REPLACES models/User.md with the generated note. Verified empirically in scratchpad: a pre-existing 'My handwritten notes about our User domain model' file was destroyed (user's note survived? false) while the log printed 'Wrote notes additively'. Silent, unrecoverable data loss of user content, contradicting the class's own guarantee.
candidates.evidence: Line 190 (write_notes, no ownership gate): `AtomicFile.write(@vault.join(rel), note)`. Class docstring lines 26-27: "guarded so it can never delete a user's own notes or run against a foreign vault." warn_foreign line 360: "'Wrote notes additively; skipped config and the stale-note sweep.'" AtomicFile.write ends with `File.rename(tmp.path, path)` — an unconditional replace. Empirical run: result {exported: 2, ...}, user's pre-existing models/User.md content gone.
candidates.suggested_fix: In write_notes (and write_indexes), when the vault is not owned, skip paths that already exist and were not woods-managed at start (check managed_marker? before overwriting an existing file), counting them as errors/skips — or refuse to write into a foreign vault entirely without an explicit flag. At minimum stop calling the behavior 'additive'.

candidates.title: Glob metacharacters in the vault path silently disable the stale-note sweep
candidates.failure_scenario: Vault path contains any Dir.glob metacharacter — brackets/braces are common in real folder names (e.g. '~/Obsidian/Work [Client]' or 'vaults [test]'). managed_notes interpolates the vault path into the glob pattern, so '[test]' is treated as a character class, the pattern matches nothing, managed_notes returns [], and sweep silently deletes nothing every run. Renamed/removed units leave stale duplicate notes and broken-topology wikilinks forever, with the result hash reporting swept: 0 and no error. Verified empirically: vault at 'vaults [test]' left Delta.md/Epsilon.md behind (swept: 0) while an identical run in a plain path swept 2. Specs only use clean mktmpdir paths, so the suite stays green (fake-vs-real filesystem gap).
candidates.evidence: Line 288: `Dir.glob(@vault.join('**', '*.md')).filter_map do |abs|` — the base path is interpolated into the pattern unescaped. Empirical: "T1 second export: {:swept=>0, ...}; stale notes remaining: [\"Delta.md\", \"Epsilon.md\"]" vs control "T2 ... swept=>2 ... stale remaining: []".
candidates.suggested_fix: Use the base: keyword so the vault path is never glob-expanded: `Dir.glob(File.join('**', '*.md'), base: @vault.to_s)` and build the absolute path with `@vault.join(rel)` afterwards.

candidates.title: frontmatter_head's YAML.safe_load raises Psych::DisallowedClass on date-typed properties, making user-touched notes permanently unsweepable
candidates.failure_scenario: A user adds a Date property (e.g. 'reviewed') to a woods note via Obsidian's Properties UI — Obsidian writes it unquoted ('reviewed: 2024-05-03'). Psych implicitly resolves that scalar to Date, and YAML.safe_load without permitted_classes raises Psych::DisallowedClass; managed_marker? rescues StandardError and returns false, so the note is no longer recognized as woods-managed. When the unit is later removed/renamed, the stale note is never swept (and it's also excluded from the purge-guard denominator). Verified empirically: after inserting 'reviewed: 2024-05-03' into a note's frontmatter, re-export reported swept: 0 and the stale note remained.
candidates.evidence: Line 318: `return YAML.safe_load(lines.join) if line == "---\n"` — no permitted_classes. Lines 300-303: `fm.is_a?(Hash) && fm['woods_managed'] == true` / `rescue StandardError` / `false`. Empirical: "T4 date-edited stale note swept? false (result: {:swept=>0, ...})".
candidates.suggested_fix: Load with `YAML.safe_load(lines.join, permitted_classes: [Date, Time], aliases: true)`, or avoid full-document parsing and only look for a literal `woods_managed: true` line within the fence.

candidates.title: Ownership sentinel is written last, so an interrupted first export permanently demotes the vault to 'foreign'
candidates.failure_scenario: First export into a fresh directory: vault_owned_at_start? is true (empty dir), notes are written, then the run dies before write_owned_assets — Ctrl-C during a large vault, disk full, or any unrescued exception in write_indexes/write_sidecar (unlike write_notes, those passes have no per-item rescue, e.g. one ENOSPC in AtomicFile aborts export_all). The .woods-vault sentinel is never created. Every subsequent run sees a non-empty vault with no sentinel, returns owned=false, and permanently runs in foreign mode: stale-note sweep and .obsidian config are skipped forever and a 'not a woods-owned vault' warning is printed for a vault woods itself created, until the user manually creates the sentinel or deletes the vault.
candidates.evidence: Sentinel written only at the end of write_owned_assets, lines 253-254: `AtomicFile.write(@vault.join(SENTINEL), ...)`, which export_all calls after write_notes/write_indexes/write_sidecar (lines 86-89). Ownership test lines 351-356 requires the sentinel or an empty dir: `(@vault.children.map { |c| c.basename.to_s } - [SENTINEL]).empty?`. write_indexes (201-208) and write_sidecar (233-242) contain no rescue.
candidates.suggested_fix: Write the sentinel immediately after computing `owned = vault_owned_at_start?` (when owned is true), before any note passes, so a crashed run remains recognizable as woods-owned on the next export.

candidates.title: FORM_ACTION_HELPER does not stop at `do`/`end` as documented — false :form_action edges in any source without `%` characters
candidates.failure_scenario:
The comment claims the regex 'Scans only within the form opening tag (up to the first `do`, `%>`, or `end`)' but `[^%]*?` only stops at a literal `%` — and it matches newlines. In ERB this accidentally works because `%>` contains `%`, but scan_form_dependencies is called on plain-Ruby sources (mailer_extractor.rb:235, phlex_extractor.rb:261, view_component_extractor.rb:309) and HAML/Slim templates where `%` may not appear for hundreds of lines. Verified: source "= form_with model: @post do |f|
  = f.text_field :name
  = f.submit
= link_to 'Dashboard', dashboard_path
" (form has NO url helper; an unrelated link_to follows the block) produces [{type: :controller, target: "DashboardController", via: :form_action}] — a fabricated form-submission edge to a controller the form never posts to.
candidates.evidence: FORM_ACTION_HELPER = /form_(with|for)\b[^%]*?(\w+)_(path|url)/   # [^%] matches newlines, `do`, `end` — nothing in the regex implements the documented boundary. Empirical scan result: [["with", "dashboard", "path"]].
candidates.suggested_fix: Bound the window to the opening line/tag: /form_(with|for)\b(?:(?!\bdo\b|%|\n).)*?(\w+)_(path|url)/ (stop at `do`, `%`, or newline). If multiline form openings must be supported, use a tempered scan that stops at `\bdo\b` and `end` tokens as the comment promises.

candidates.title: Job enqueues chained through .set(...) are never detected — no :job dependency edge and no jobs_enqueued side effect
candidates.failure_scenario: `NotificationJob.set(wait: 5.minutes).perform_later(user)` — the canonical ActiveJob idiom for delayed/queue-overridden enqueue — matches neither `/(\w+Job)\.perform/` (scan_job_dependencies, used by model/concern/policy/state-machine/graphql extractors) nor CallbackAnalyzer::ASYNC_PATTERN (callback_analyzer.rb:46, `/(\w+(?:Job|Worker))\.(?:perform_later|...)/`), because both require the async method to immediately follow the class name. Verified: scan_job_dependencies("NotificationJob.set(wait: 5.minutes).perform_later(user)\nPlainJob.perform_later(x)") returns only [{type: :job, target: "PlainJob", via: :code_reference}]. Result: every scheduled/queued-with-options job is invisible in the dependency graph, and callback side-effect analysis ('what happens when X runs?' — the gem's core promise) omits those enqueues entirely.
candidates.evidence: source.scan(/(\w+Job)\.perform/).flatten...   (shared_dependency_scanner.rb:172) and ASYNC_PATTERN = /(\w+(?:Job|Worker))\.(?:#{ASYNC_METHODS...})/ (callback_analyzer.rb:46) — neither allows an intervening `.set(...)`. Empirical: NotificationJob edge missing from scan output.
candidates.suggested_fix: Allow an optional set-chain in both patterns: /(\w+Job)(?:\.set\([^)]*\))?\.perform/ and /(\w+(?:Job|Worker))(?:\.set\([^)]*\))?\.(?:perform_later|perform_async|perform_in|perform_at)/. Same treatment for Sidekiq's `.perform_in`-style `SomeWorker.set(queue: ...)` chains.

candidates.title: extract_initialize_params reports tokens from default-value expressions as parameters (and misses positional defaults)
candidates.failure_scenario: For `def initialize(service = UserService.new, role = :admin)` the scan `params_str.scan(/(\w+)(?::\s*([^,\n]+))?/)` matches EVERY word token in the parameter string, not just parameter names. Verified output: [{name: "service", has_default: false, ...}, {name: "UserService", ...}, {name: "new", ...}, {name: "role", has_default: false, ...}, {name: "admin", ...}] — three phantom parameters (UserService, new, admin) and both real positional defaults reported as has_default: false (the capture group only recognizes keyword-style `name: default`). This garbage lands in metadata[:initialize_params] for every service, policy, manager, poro, lib, and decorator unit (service_extractor.rb:118, policy_extractor.rb:110, manager_extractor.rb:115, poro_extractor.rb:208, lib_extractor.rb:196, decorator_extractor.rb:164), so retrieval/LLM consumers see a fabricated constructor signature.
candidates.evidence: params_str.scan(/(\w+)(?::\s*([^,\n]+))?/) do |name, default|   # \w+ matches words inside default expressions too. Empirical: 5 'params' returned for a 2-param initialize, all has_default: false.
candidates.suggested_fix: Split on top-level commas first (e.g. params_str.split(/,(?![^(\[{]*[)\]}])/)), then for each segment take the leading identifier via /\A\s*\*{0,2}&?(\w+)/, set has_default from presence of `=` or a value after `:`, and keyword from a trailing `:` on the name token.

candidates.title: strip_line_comment treats `#` inside regex literals as a comment, truncating the line and dropping real model references
candidates.failure_scenario: The comment-stripper tracks only single/double-quote state, so a `#` inside a regex literal starts a 'comment'. Verified: strip_line_comment("phone.gsub(/#/, '') && Article.touch_all\n") returns "phone.gsub(/\n" — the `Article` reference is silently dropped, so scan_model_dependencies (which runs every pass over the stripped source, line 58) emits no edge for it. Real-world triggers: hex-color regexes (/\A#\h{6}\z/), hashtag/anchor stripping (sub(/#.*/,'')), fragment parsing — any line where a model/service/job constant follows a regex containing `#`. This directly violates the method's own contract at lines 88-90 ('mis-reading one only risks a spurious edge... never... a dropped-but-real reference outside those constructs') — regex literals are not in the enumerated tradeoff list and the dropped reference is ordinary code outside the construct.
candidates.evidence:
elsif ch == '#'
  trailing = line[i..].end_with?("
") ? "
" : ''
  return line[0...i] + trailing   # no regex-literal state; empirical result: "phone.gsub(/
" for input "phone.gsub(/#/, '') && Article.touch_all
".
candidates.suggested_fix: Add regex-literal tracking to the state walker: enter regex mode on `/` when the previous non-space char is one of `( , = ~ ! ; & | [ {` or line start, exit on unescaped `/`; treat `#` inside as literal. A cheaper mitigation matching Ruby convention: only treat `#` as a comment when at line start or preceded by whitespace, which keeps `gsub(/#/, ...)` intact at the cost of leaving rare `x#comment` unstripped (a spurious-edge risk the docs already accept).

candidates.title: YAML.safe_load without aliases: true raises Psych::AliasesNotEnabled on anchor/alias locale and schedule files — silently dropped though Rails loads them fine
candidates.failure_scenario: config/locales/en.yml using the extremely common anchor pattern (shared blocks like 'defaults: &defaults' + '<<: *defaults', or en-GB aliasing en) parses fine in the running app — the i18n backend loads YAML with aliases enabled — but I18nExtractor's YAML.safe_load(source, permitted_classes: [...]) raises Psych::AliasesNotEnabled (verified on Psych 5.1.2; Psych 3 raises Psych::BadAlias), which the 'rescue StandardError' turns into nil: the entire locale file vanishes from the index with only a log line. Same defect at scheduled_job_extractor.rb:96 (YAML.safe_load(source, permitted_classes: [Symbol])) where env-keyed recurring.yml/sidekiq_cron.yml files conventionally use 'production: &production' + 'staging:\n  <<: *production' — all scheduled jobs silently dropped. Fake-vs-real gap: alias-free spec fixtures keep tests green.
candidates.evidence: i18n_extractor.rb:48: 'data = YAML.safe_load(source, permitted_classes: [Symbol, Date, Time, Regexp])' with line 67 'rescue StandardError => e ... nil'. scheduled_job_extractor.rb:96: 'data = YAML.safe_load(source, permitted_classes: [Symbol])' with line 78 'rescue StandardError ... []'. Empirical: YAML.safe_load on 'defaults: &defaults ... <<: *defaults' => RAISED: Psych::AliasesNotEnabled: Alias parsing was not enabled.
candidates.suggested_fix: Pass aliases: true to both safe_load calls (guard for Psych < 3.1 if the support floor demands: rescue ArgumentError and retry without the kwarg). Matches how Rails/i18n actually load these files; content is still restricted by permitted_classes.

candidates.title: block_opener? matches keywords inside comments/strings/trailing modifiers, permanently corrupting depth: later tasks get wrong namespaces and block bodies overrun
candidates.failure_scenario: Any rake file containing a comment or string with a bare keyword — '# do not run this in production', 'puts "waiting for input"' (\bfor\b), 'sleep 1 while busy?' — increments depth with no matching 'end', so namespace_depths never re-align. Verified end-to-end on the real extractor: a file with 'namespace :reports do', a '# do not run this in production' comment, then a top-level 'task :cleanup' AFTER the namespace closes yields task full_name 'reports:cleanup' instead of 'cleanup' — wrong identifier, wrong namespace, wrong MCP retrieval key. extract_task_block uses the same predicate, so block bodies run past their real 'end' (misattributing Rake::Task invocations from later tasks as dependencies). Also 'end # comment' never decrements (stripped == 'end' exact match).
candidates.evidence: Line 253: "return true if stripped.match?(/\\b(do|def|case|begin|class|module|while|until|for)\\b.*(?<!\\bend)\\s*$/)" — no comment/string exclusion, keywords matched anywhere in the line. Empirical: block_opener?("# do the deletion for each batch") => true; block_opener?('puts "waiting for input"') => true; parse_tasks on the reports/cleanup fixture => task="reports:cleanup" (expected "cleanup").
candidates.suggested_fix: In both parse_tasks and extract_task_block: skip lines where stripped.start_with?('#'); treat only trailing block-forms as openers (e.g. /\bdo\s*(\|[^|]*\|)?\s*$/ for do-blocks, /\A(def|class|module|case|begin)\b/ for keyword blocks); relax the end check to /\Aend\b/. This keeps the line-based heuristic but stops comments/strings from shifting depth.

candidates.title: extract_cache_calls stamps the file's FIRST cache key and FIRST TTL onto every call entry, across call types
candidates.failure_scenario: A controller with 'Rails.cache.fetch("products/all")' in one action and 'Rails.cache.write("stats/daily", ..., expires_in: 5.minutes)' plus 'Rails.cache.delete("stats/stale")' in another produces cache_calls metadata where all three entries carry key_pattern '"products/all"' (the write and delete never touch that key) and all three carry ttl '5.minutes' (the fetch has no TTL). Verified against the real extractor: [{type: :fetch, key_pattern: '"products/all"', ttl: '5.minutes'}, {type: :write, key_pattern: '"products/all"', ...}, {type: :delete, key_pattern: '"products/all"', ...}]. Any file with 2+ cache calls — the normal case — gets factually wrong per-call metadata in the index, misleading agents reasoning about cache keys/TTLs.
candidates.evidence: Lines 169-174: 'CACHE_PATTERNS.each do |type, pattern|; source.scan(pattern) do; key = extract_key_pattern(source, type); ttl = extract_ttl(source)' — the scan block ignores the match position; line 190: 'match = source.match(KEY_PATTERN)' and line 199: 'match = source.match(TTL_PATTERN)' both always return the first match in the whole file, and KEY_PATTERN matches any of fetch|read|write|delete regardless of the entry's type.

candidates.title: Re-capturing a snapshot for the same git SHA orphans all prior unit-hash rows (or raises under FK enforcement) because INSERT OR REPLACE churns the snapshot id
candidates.failure_scenario: enable_snapshots = true; run `woods:extract` twice on the same commit (the normal dev loop — re-extract without committing). `upsert_snapshot` executes `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO woods_snapshots` against `UNIQUE(git_sha)` with `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` (migration 004), so SQLite deletes the old row and inserts a fresh one with a NEW id. `capture` then runs `DELETE FROM woods_snapshot_units WHERE snapshot_id = ?` with the NEW id — which matches nothing — and inserts a full new set of unit rows. The old rows, still pointing at the dead id, are orphaned forever (migration 005's `FOREIGN KEY (snapshot_id) REFERENCES woods_snapshots(id)` has no ON DELETE CASCADE, and the gem's raw `SQLite3::Database.new` connection in extractor.rb:1102 never enables `PRAGMA foreign_keys`). Verified empirically with the real class + real migrations: after 5 captures of the same SHA with 2 units, woods_snapshot_units holds 10 rows, 8 orphaned — woods.sqlite3 grows by units-count rows (thousands in a real app) on every re-extraction, unbounded. On any connection with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` (e.g. a Rails-managed SQLite connection), the second capture instead raises `SQLite3::ConstraintException: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` (also verified), which the extractor's rescue logs and swallows — snapshots silently stop updating.
candidates.evidence: snapshot_store.rb:233-238: `@db.execute(<<~SQL, params)\n  INSERT OR REPLACE INTO woods_snapshots\n    (git_sha, git_branch, ...)`; capture at :96-98: `snapshot_id = fetch_snapshot_id(git_sha)` / `@db.execute('DELETE FROM woods_snapshot_units WHERE snapshot_id = ?', [snapshot_id])` — fetch happens AFTER the replace, so it always returns the new id. Migration 005:26: `FOREIGN KEY (snapshot_id) REFERENCES woods_snapshots(id)` (no cascade). Test output: `after 1st capture: snapshot id=1, unit rows=2` / `after 2nd capture: snapshot id=2, unit rows=4, orphaned rows=2` / `after 5 captures total: unit rows=10, orphans=8` / `FK-on recapture raised: SQLite3::ConstraintException: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. Repro script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/303db451-4f45-597e-9493-349969b61c69/scratchpad/snap_test.rb
candidates.suggested_fix: Stop using INSERT OR REPLACE: look up the existing id first and UPDATE it (or use `INSERT INTO ... ON CONFLICT(git_sha) DO UPDATE SET ...`, supported by SQLite >= 3.24), so the snapshot id is stable across re-captures; alternatively delete unit rows by the OLD id before the replace. Also add ON DELETE CASCADE in migration 005 for defense in depth.

candidates.title: Stale-lock takeover loser vacates the lock path before restoring it — a third process acquires in the window, producing two concurrent lock holders
candidates.failure_scenario: Three agents contend after a crashed run left a stale lock (the exact multi-agent scenario this class exists for). P1 and P2 both pass `stale?` on the old file. P1 wins: retires the stale lock and O_EXCL-creates a fresh one — P1 legitimately holds. P2 resumes: its `File.rename(@lock_path, graveyard)` (line 150) moves P1's FRESH lock aside; `stale_file?` correctly detects freshness and P2 heads for `restore_lock` — but between the rename and the `File.link` restore (line 188), the lock path is VACANT. P3's `acquire` during that window sees no file and O_EXCL-creates its own lock. P2's link then gets EEXIST and discards P1's lock file. Result: P1 and P3 both run their pipeline critical sections concurrently — two simultaneous `woods:extract` runs interleaving writes into the same output dir, precisely what the lock must prevent. Verified with the real class (only a pause injected between the rename and the restore): output `P1 acquire: true / P3 acquire during P2's restore window: true / DOUBLE HOLD: true`. The identical rename→inspect→restore vacancy exists in `release` (lines 82→92): after a legitimate takeover, the old holder's release vacates the new holder's lock path before restoring it.
candidates.evidence: retire_stale_lock: `graveyard = "#{@lock_path}.stale.#{Process.pid}..."; File.rename(@lock_path, graveyard)` (line 150) then `unless stale_file?(graveyard) ... restore_lock(graveyard); return false` (lines 152-157) — the path is empty between these; restore_lock: `File.link(graveyard, @lock_path) rescue Errno::EEXIST` (lines 188-191) explicitly yields to "a newer holder" — but that newer holder (P3) acquired while P1 still holds. Same shape in release: `File.rename(@lock_path, graveyard)` (line 82) ... `restore_lock(graveyard)` (line 92). Repro: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/303db451-4f45-597e-9493-349969b61c69/scratchpad/lock_test.rb prints `DOUBLE HOLD: true`.
candidates.suggested_fix: Never let a non-holder vacate the path. Break stale locks without rename: open the existing lock file, flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) it, re-verify staleness by fstat on the OPEN fd (immune to replacement), and unlink via the still-flocked fd's path only if the inode matches (compare File.stat(path).ino to fd.stat.ino) — competitors serialize on the flock instead of racing renames. Similarly make release verify ownership by reading first and unlinking only after an inode match, or hold a long-lived flock for the whole with_lock lifetime.

candidates.title: GapDetector counts word occurrences, not distinct queries — one low-score query repeating a word fabricates a 'repeated low scores' pattern and misstates the count
candidates.failure_scenario: Two rating entries exist (satisfying `low_ratings.size >= MIN_PATTERN_COUNT`), one of them the query "user user user avatar" with score 1. `count_keywords` increments the counter once per word occurrence inside a single query, so counts['user'] = 3 from ONE query. `detect` then emits `{type: :repeated_low_scores, count: 3, description: "3 low-score queries mention 'user'"}` — a false pattern (only 1 query mentions 'user', not 3) crossing the MIN_PATTERN_COUNT=2 threshold that is supposed to require repetition ACROSS queries. Verified empirically: with ratings ["user user user avatar" (1), "checkout flow" (2)], detect prints `3 low-score queries mention 'user'`. Agents consuming the MCP feedback/gap tools get told to prioritize a nonexistent coverage gap, and the reported count is wrong whenever any query repeats a keyword.
candidates.evidence: Lines 61-66: `counts = Hash.new(0); ratings.each do |rating|; words = rating['query'].to_s.downcase.split(/\W+/).reject { |w| w.length < 3 }; words.each { |w| counts[w] += 1 }` — no per-query dedup; line 46/51: `keyword_counts.select { |_, count| count >= MIN_PATTERN_COUNT }` ... `description: "#{count} low-score queries mention '#{keyword}'"`. Verified output: `3 low-score queries mention 'user'` from a corpus where exactly one low-score query contains 'user'.
candidates.suggested_fix: Dedupe per query: `words.uniq.each { |w| counts[w] += 1 }` (or `words.to_set`), so the count means "number of distinct low-score queries containing the keyword", matching the description and the MIN_PATTERN_COUNT semantics.

candidates.title: Stale non-probe failures arriving while the circuit is :open keep resetting @last_failure_time, postponing the half_open recovery probe indefinitely
candidates.failure_scenario: threshold=5, reset_timeout=60. During an outage, 20 threads are already in-flight (admitted while :closed) against a hung service with staggered 55s timeouts. The 5th failure opens the circuit at T. The class's own doc says stale pre-outage calls "must not decide recovery" — and record_failure/record_success correctly ignore them in :half_open — but in :open there is no guard: each straggler's failure runs `@last_failure_time = monotonic_now`, so `reset_timeout_elapsed?` ("monotonic_now - @last_failure_time >= @reset_timeout") keeps restarting. With stragglers failing every <60s, the open→half_open transition is postponed until 60s after the LAST stale call dies — minutes past the configured reset_timeout even if the service recovered immediately after the circuit opened. RetryableProvider stacked on the same breaker amplifies this: every waiting caller keeps getting CircuitOpenError long after recovery, with `@failure_count` also inflated by the stale calls (misreported in the error message '#{@failure_count} failures').
candidates.evidence: record_failure (lines 143-150): `return if @state == :half_open && !probing` — the only stale-call guard; then unconditionally `@failure_count += 1; @last_failure_time = monotonic_now; ...` even when `@state == :open` and `probing` is false. reset_timeout_elapsed? (line 124): `@last_failure_time && (monotonic_now - @last_failure_time >= @reset_timeout)`. Contrast the stated invariant at lines 137-140: a stale call "is not the probe and must not decide recovery (its outcome reflects the pre-outage attempt, not the current one)" — yet in :open it does exactly that by moving the recovery deadline.
candidates.suggested_fix: In record_failure, also skip timer/counter updates for non-probe calls once the circuit is no longer :closed: `return if @state != :closed && !probing` (keeping the probing half_open reopen path, which should refresh @last_failure_time). Stale failures then neither inflate @failure_count nor push back the recovery window.

candidates.title: JsonSnapshotStore calls FileUtils.mkdir_p but never requires 'fileutils' — NameError when loaded without another file having loaded it first
candidates.failure_scenario: The file's requires are only 'json', 'time', 'digest' (lines 3-5), yet the constructor runs `FileUtils.mkdir_p(@dir)`. Any process that loads this file per its own documented usage (`store = JsonSnapshotStore.new(dir: '/app/tmp/woods')` after a bare require) crashes with `NameError: uninitialized constant Woods::Temporal::JsonSnapshotStore::FileUtils`. Verified empirically: `ruby --disable-gems -e '...require "woods/temporal/json_snapshot_store"; JsonSnapshotStore.new(dir: ...)'` → `NameError: uninitialized constant ... FileUtils`; also confirmed plain `ruby -e` (rubygems enabled) does NOT preload FileUtils. Today it works by accident on the two in-gem paths (extractor runs under Rails where ActiveSupport loads fileutils; the MCP bootstrapper transitively requires index_artifact.rb which requires 'fileutils'), so any refactor of those require chains — the exact fake-vs-real trap this audit targets — turns snapshot fallback construction into a boot crash.
candidates.evidence: Lines 3-5: `require 'json'` / `require 'time'` / `require 'digest'` — no fileutils; line 27: `FileUtils.mkdir_p(@dir)`. Verified: `NameError: uninitialized constant Woods::Temporal::JsonSnapshotStore::FileUtils` and `FileUtils NOT loaded under plain ruby`.
candidates.suggested_fix: Add `require 'fileutils'` to the file's header (matching sibling files like coordination/pipeline_lock.rb and feedback/store.rb which correctly require it).
